subject: Communication
title: The Fight-or-Flight Response on Stage
description: One-minute skill: The Fight-or-Flight Response on Stage.

hook.text: Your hands shake, your mouth dries, your heart races. You're not dying — you're about to give a speech.

buildup.text: Your amygdala detected a threat (the audience) and flooded your body with adrenaline and cortisol.

discovery.text: Blood flows away from your brain to your muscles. That's why you forget your lines — literally.

twist.text: Harvard research found that reframing anxiety as excitement uses the same hormones more effectively.

climax.text: Saying 'I'm excited' before speaking measurably improves performance over saying 'I'm calm.'

punchline.text: Don't fight the adrenaline. Rename it.

quiz.question: What did Harvard research suggest about reframing stage anxiety?

details.summary: When a speaker steps on stage, their sympathetic nervous system floods the body with adrenaline and cortisol. Heart rate rises, palms sweat, and muscles tense. This ancient survival mechanism can be channeled into dynamic energy rather than frozen paralysis with the right techniques.
details.whyItMatters: The physical symptoms of stage fright are identical to excitement. Reframing the response transforms a liability into a performance advantage.
takeaways: Adrenaline increases heart rate, alertness, and energy
The symptoms of fear and excitement are physiologically identical
Reframing anxiety as excitement improves performance

faq.question: How can speakers channel nervousness into energy?
faq.answer: Tell yourself you are excited rather than scared. Harvard research shows that saying I am excited out loud before a performance shifts the brain from a threat mindset to an opportunity mindset, improving actual performance measurably.

faq.question: Why do experienced speakers still get nervous?
faq.answer: The fight-or-flight response never fully disappears because it is hardwired. Even veteran performers report pre-stage anxiety. The difference is they have learned to interpret the sensation as readiness rather than danger and use the energy to enhance their delivery.
